title: Intervals in music
description: Memorize scale and chord interval recipes, melodic vs harmonic hearing, and open-chord breakdowns.

cards.front: What is a melodic interval? A harmonic interval?
cards.back: Melodic: two notes one after the other; the ear follows motion up or down. Harmonic: two notes sounded together; the ear hears a blend.

cards.front: How can the same interval appear both melodically and harmonically?
cards.back: A chord is a harmonic stack; an arpeggio plays the same chord melodically. A scale is a sequence of melodic intervals from a tonic.

cards.front: What intervals above the tonic make a major scale?
What intervals above the tonic make a natural minor scale?
Give the intervals above the root for major, minor, diminished, and augmented triads.
cards.back: Major: M3, P5. Minor: m3, P5. Diminished: m3, d5. Augmented: M3, A5.

cards.front: What intervals above the root make a dominant 7th chord?
How are major and minor triads built as stacks of adjacent thirds?
cards.back: Major: M3 then m3. Minor: m3 then M3.

cards.front: Does an interval have a fixed emotion, such as “bright” for a major 3rd?
cards.back: No. Mood words are common associations in a style, not properties of the interval. A major chord can sound ominous; a minor chord can sound cheerful. Train size, not feelings.

cards.front: Which intervals does traditional Western theory treat as stable vs tense?
cards.back: Stable: unisons, P5s, P4s (depending on context), 3rds, 6ths, octaves. Tense: 2nds, 7ths, and the tritone. Stability in practice still depends on what the music does with the interval.

cards.front: Do an ascending P5 and a descending P5 sound the same?
cards.back: Same size, different sound and feel. A P4 up and a P4 down likewise differ. Direction matters.

cards.front: How do the 3rd and 5th give a triad its color?
cards.back: The 3rd decides major or minor. The 5th provides stability; a d5 makes a diminished sound, an A5 an augmented sound.

cards.front: In G7 (G B D F), which notes form a tritone, and how does traditional tonal music often resolve it toward C?
cards.back: B and F form a d5. That tension often resolves inward: B up to C, F down to E (a major 3rd), which is part of why G7 pulls toward C. A learned convention; many styles treat the chord differently.

cards.front: What interval starts “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”? The “Jaws” motif?
cards.back: Twinkle (C C G G) is a perfect 5th up. Jaws (E to F) is a minor 2nd up. Useful aids, not the only way to hear size.

cards.front: In open A major, name each note from low to high and its interval above A2.
cards.back: String 5 open A2 unison; string 4 fret 2 E3 P5; string 3 fret 2 A3 P8; string 2 fret 2 C♯4 M10 (M3 plus an octave); string 1 open E4 P12 (P5 plus an octave).

cards.front: In open A major, what happens if you move string 2 from fret 2 to fret 1?
cards.back: C♯ becomes C♮. The M3 becomes a m3 and the chord changes from A major to A minor. Every other interval stays the same.

cards.front: For A C♯ E, give the intervals above A and the interval between C♯ and E.
cards.back: Above A: M3 and P5. C♯ to E is a minor 3rd (the upper adjacent third of a major triad).

cards.front: Build a minor triad on D by intervals (root, m3, P5).
Name the intervals in a diminished triad on B: B D F.
cards.back: B to D is a minor 3rd; D to F is a minor 3rd; B to F is a diminished 5th.

cards.front: Open E minor notes E B E G B E (strings 6 to 1). Give each interval above E2.
cards.back: Unison, P5, P8, m10, P12, two octaves (P15).
